opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the more serious objections, and I take it seriously. It's actually one of the main things that's caused me to lengthen my timelines a bit over the past year or two.

The basic argument goes something like this: current models are incredibly data-inefficient compared to humans. A human kid learns language from maybe tens of millions of words, while these models need trillions of tokens. And once a model is deployed, it basically doesn't learn on the job the way a human employee does. A new hire at a company is pretty mediocre in their first week, but after six months they've picked up all this context and tacit knowledge, they've learned from their mistakes. Current AI systems mostly don't do that. They have a context window, but that's a pretty poor substitute for actual learning. So the worry is that until we crack these problems, AIs will stay stuck as impressive-but-brittle tools that can't really substitute for a researcher doing long-horizon work, and maybe cracking them requires some fundamental paradigm shift that could take decades.

Here's how I think about it. First, I agree these are real limitations. I don't think you can just hand-wave them away. But I think there are a few reasons not to expect them to delay things for decades.

One is that you don't necessarily need to solve data efficiency or online learning in a human-like way to get to an intelligence explosion. What you need is AI systems that are good enough at AI research specifically, especially the coding and experiment-running parts, to substantially speed up the research process. And AI research is a domain where we can generate enormous amounts of training data and get relatively clean feedback signals. Did the code run, did the experiment improve the metric, and so forth. So you might be able to brute-force your way to superhuman coding and research engineering even with relatively inefficient learning, because the inefficiency can be compensated for with scale and with RL environments.

Two, once you have that, the automated researchers themselves can work on the data efficiency and online learning problems. So these limitations might be things that get solved during the takeoff rather than prerequisites for it.

Three, there's been real progress on adjacent things: longer context, better memory scaffolding, models that can do longer and longer tasks autonomously. The trend in task horizon length has been pretty steady. Whether that trend continues is a big question, but extrapolating it doesn't obviously point to decades.

That said, I'd put meaningful probability on the pessimistic view. If it turns out that getting to really robust long-horizon agency requires something like genuine continual learning, and nobody finds a good way to do that within the current paradigm, then yeah, things could stall for a while. Maybe compute scaling also slows down around the end of the decade because it gets too expensive, and then you're relying on algorithmic progress alone, which is slower. In that world, it could be a long time.

So my overall take is: it's a real consideration, it shifts some probability mass later, but I don't think it's a strong reason to be confident things are decades away. The central scenario I worry about is still that things move quite fast, and I think it would be a mistake to treat this objection as grounds for complacency.

r001.rationale: The response says scale and RL can compensate for poor data efficiency and that automated researchers may solve the problem during takeoff, but it does not frame data efficiency as a metric improved through iterative optimization.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says data efficiency and online learning need not be solved in a human-like way to reach an intelligence explosion.

r003.rationale: The response describes a possible decades-long stall if robust agency requires continual learning and no solution is found, but it does not call for an argument explaining persistence despite rapid progress and recent paradigm shifts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is probably the single best argument for longer timelines, and I want to give it its due before I say why I don't fully buy it.

The argument goes something like: current models are wildly sample-inefficient compared to humans. A human learns to be a competent software engineer or researcher from, you know, a few years of experience, a few thousand hours of doing the thing. Models need training on the equivalent of millions of lifetimes of text, and even then they don't really learn on the job the way a person does. You can't drop one into a company and have it get better at that company's problems over six months the way a new hire does. Everything is sort of baked in at training time, plus whatever fits in the context window. And if you think that gap is fundamental, if you think there's some missing ingredient for continual learning that we just don't have, then you could tell a story where we stall out. We get really impressive systems that are nonetheless stuck at "very good at tasks that look like their training data" and we spend decades grinding on the missing piece.

I take that seriously. If I had to point to one thing that could make my timelines wrong, it's roughly this.

But here's why I don't think it buys you decades. First, the gap has been closing. Sample efficiency has improved a lot over the past several years, through better architectures, better data curation, RL on reasoning, and so on. It's not like we've been stuck. Second, you don't actually need human-level sample efficiency to get an intelligence explosion. You need systems that are good enough at AI research to meaningfully accelerate the search for whatever the missing ingredients are. And AI research is weirdly well-suited to current systems, because so much of it is writing code, running experiments, reading papers, iterating. If you have a million copies of something that's roughly as good as a solid ML researcher at those tasks, even if each one is individually brittle and can't learn on the job, you can throw enormous amounts of parallel effort at the continual learning problem itself. That's the thing people miss. The bottleneck gets attacked by the thing that's bottlenecked.

Third, there are workarounds that don't require solving the problem elegantly. Long context, retrieval, fine-tuning on the fly, periodic retraining on everything that happened last week. These are hacky, but hacky can carry you pretty far if you have enough compute, and compute is what the labs are buying.

So my honest view is: this could add a year or two, maybe a few years, to how long it takes to get to the point where AI is substantially automating AI research. I'd put real probability on it mattering. But "decades" requires believing both that the problem is deeply hard and that nothing short of a clean solution will do, and I don't think either of those is well supported. The thing I'd watch is whether we see models getting better at long-horizon agentic tasks and at actually improving over the course of extended engagements. If that flatlines for a couple of years, I'd update a lot. If it keeps climbing the way it has, I think the data efficiency argument mostly dissolves.

r001.rationale: It says sample efficiency has improved over recent years through better architectures, data curation, and reasoning RL, presenting it as something that can improve through continued optimization.

r002.rationale: It says human-level sample efficiency is not required to start an intelligence explosion: AI researchers could accelerate work on the missing ingredients even if systems cannot learn on the job.

r003.rationale: It sketches a possible decades-long stall if continual learning is fundamentally missing, but does not explain why that obstacle would persist despite rapid progress or why recent advances would fail to resolve it.

astra-6.text:
I think those are real uncertainties, but I’m skeptical that they buy us decades. It’s useful to distinguish between “there are important things current systems can’t do” and “those things will take decades to figure out.” The first doesn’t establish the second.

Take data efficiency. An AI system doesn’t necessarily have to learn as efficiently as a human to automate AI research. It can compensate with more training data and compute. And in domains where you can run experiments and check the results, you can generate additional useful data. That doesn’t make data constraints disappear, but it means we need to ask which particular capabilities are bottlenecked by which kinds of data.

Similarly, online learning could turn out to be a serious obstacle. But there’s a question about how much of it you need. A system can learn things within its context, record results, and use those results in subsequent work, even if its underlying weights aren’t changing continuously. Then you can periodically train an improved version. That might be less efficient than human learning, but it could still support a feedback loop where AI systems help build better AI systems.

The strongest version of the objection, I think, is that progress requires experience or experiments that simply take a long time. You can’t necessarily compress a year of observing the world into a day by thinking faster. That could substantially slow some kinds of progress. But to delay an intelligence explosion for decades, those constraints would have to bind quite strongly on AI research itself, despite the ability to run experiments in parallel and do a lot of the work in software.

So I wouldn’t dismiss these arguments. They’re reasons for uncertainty about how fast the process goes. I just don’t think pointing to limitations in today’s systems is enough to justify confidence in a decades-long delay.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compensating for data limits with more data and compute, but does not frame data efficiency as a metric improved through iterative optimization.

r002.rationale: It says continuous weight updates may not be needed: systems can use context and recorded results, then periodically train improved versions while supporting a feedback loop.

r003.rationale: It says a decades-long delay would require constraints to bind strongly on AI research, but does not call for explaining their persistence despite rapid AI progress and recent paradigm shifts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those are real bottlenecks to consider, but I’m skeptical that they buy us decades. We should distinguish between saying, “You can’t just run a model faster and expect it to become smarter,” which seems right, and saying, “It’ll take decades for AI systems to learn how to do substantially better AI research.” That second claim needs a much stronger argument.

Suppose you have AI systems that are roughly as good as human researchers at improving AI. Even if those systems can’t continuously update their own weights, they can still run experiments, read the results, write code, and contribute to training the next generation. The learning can happen at the level of the research process rather than inside each individual model. That’s already how a lot of human progress works: individual researchers don’t need to become dramatically smarter for the field to advance.

Data efficiency matters because some experiments require collecting new information, and some information is expensive or slow to obtain. So I don’t think we should assume that a million copies of a researcher produce a million times as much progress. You’ll have diminishing returns and bottlenecks in compute and experimentation.

But to get a delay of decades, you need those bottlenecks to remain binding even as the systems get better at finding ways around them. That’s possible, but it’s not something I’d feel comfortable counting on. My uncertainty is more about how fast the feedback loop runs and where it starts to slow down than about whether online learning is a necessary prerequisite for it to get going.

r001.rationale: It says data efficiency matters because some information is costly or slow to obtain, but does not frame it as a metric improved through iterative optimization.

r002.rationale: It says AI research can advance through experiments, results, and code even if individual models cannot continuously update their weights, so online learning need not be a prerequisite for the feedback loop to start.

r003.rationale: It says a decades-long delay would require bottlenecks to remain binding as systems improve, but does not address recent paradigm shifts or explicitly call for an argument accounting for them.
